objectives: Parametrise a test over a table of cases

screens.title: Four checks, one result
screens.prose:
This test checks a buggy `max_drawdown` four times. pytest reports `FAILED test_max_drawdown`, pointing at the first `assert`.

```python
def test_max_drawdown():
    assert max_drawdown([100.00, 120.00, 90.00]) == pytest.approx(-0.25)
    assert max_drawdown([100.00, 110.00]) == 0.0
    assert max_drawdown([80.00, 60.00, 70.00]) == pytest.approx(-0.25)
    assert max_drawdown([50.00]) == 0.0
```
screens.question: What do you know about the other three cases?

options.why: You read one failure as 'the rest are fine'. A failed `assert` stops the function, so the lines after it never run.
You read one failure as 'all failed'. The later lines never ran, so pytest has no result for them.

hints.text: What does a failed `assert` do to the rest of the function?
It raises `AssertionError`, which ends the function on that line.

feedback.correct: The first failure ended the function, so three cases have no result.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what happens after an `assert` fails.

byKey.passed: You read one failure as 'the rest are fine'. The function stopped at the first `assert`, so the other three never ran.

explain.text: The first `assert` raised `AssertionError` and the function stopped there. Three of the four cases were never checked, so one bug can hide another. We want each case to run and report on its own.

screens.title: A parametrised test
screens.prose:
pytest builds that table for us. This is a **parametrised** test: one function, run once per row.

```python
@pytest.mark.parametrize("prices, expected", [
    ([100.00, 120.00, 90.00], -0.25),
    ([100.00, 110.00], 0.0),
    ([80.00, 60.00, 70.00], -0.25),
    ([50.00], 0.0),
])
def test_max_drawdown(prices, expected):
    assert max_drawdown(prices) == pytest.approx(expected)
```
screens.question: With the first-price bug, what does pytest's last line say?

options.why: You counted one function as one test. Each row is its own test, so the other three still run and pass.
You expected one failing row to fail the whole function. Rows run separately, and three of them pass.

hints.text: How many tests does a table of four rows make?
Four tests. Only the first row failed on the last screen.

feedback.correct: Four rows, four tests, one failure.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count one test per row.

explain.text: The decorator names the parameters, then lists one row per case. pytest runs the function once per row and names each run with an id built from the values. A list gets its name and row number, as in `prices0`.

screens.title: Your own table
screens.prose: Turn the four-assert test into a parametrised one. Keep the name `test_max_drawdown` and the four cases. Run examples prints one line per row.
screens.question: Rewrite `test_max_drawdown` with `@pytest.mark.parametrize`.

widget.starter:
import pytest


def max_drawdown(prices):
    peak, worst = prices[0], 0.0
    for p in prices:
        peak = max(peak, p)
        worst = min(worst, p / peak - 1)
    return worst

# Rewrite this as one parametrised test with the same four cases.
def test_max_drawdown():
    assert max_drawdown([100.00, 120.00, 90.00]) == pytest.approx(-0.25)
    assert max_drawdown([100.00, 110.00]) == 0.0
    assert max_drawdown([80.00, 60.00, 70.00]) == pytest.approx(-0.25)
    assert max_drawdown([50.00]) == 0.0

tests.setup: planted = lambda prices: min(p / prices[0] - 1 for p in prices)
planted = lambda prices: max(1 - p / max(prices[:i + 1]) for i, p in enumerate(prices))
planted = lambda prices: min([0.0] + [p / max(prices[:i + 1]) - 1 for i, p in enumerate(prices[:-1])])

screens.title: A row that earns its place
screens.prose:
Another wrong version finds the highest price, then the lowest price after it:

```python
def max_drawdown(prices):
    top = max(prices)
    after = prices[prices.index(top):]
    return min(after) / top - 1
```

It passes all four rows of your table.
screens.question: Which row would catch this version?

options.why: Here the worst fall comes after the highest price, so this version gets −0.50 right too.
The highest price comes first, so 'after the top' is the whole series. It gets −0.1667 right.
The highest price is first again, so it gets −0.10 right.

hints.text: When does 'the fall after the highest price' miss the worst fall?
Look for a row whose worst fall happens before the highest price.
Row C falls to 50.00 (−0.50) before it reaches 120.00. This version only sees 110.00 / 120.00 − 1.

feedback.correct: Row C: the true answer is −0.50, and this version says −0.0833.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a row where the worst fall comes before the highest price.

explain.text: In row C the price halves, from 100.00 to 50.00, then climbs to a new high of 120.00. This version only looks after 120.00 and returns 110 / 120 − 1 ≈ −0.0833. A good row targets a mistake the other rows cannot see.

widget.solution:
import pytest


def max_drawdown(prices):
    peak, worst = prices[0], 0.0
    for p in prices:
        peak = max(peak, p)
        worst = min(worst, p / peak - 1)
    return worst

# Five fund paths, in pounds. Work out each drawdown by hand.
@pytest.mark.parametrize("prices, expected", [
    ([250.00, 262.50, 210.00, 231.00], -0.20),   # 210 / 262.5 - 1
    ([200.00, 150.00, 220.00, 209.00], -0.25),   # 150 / 200 - 1, before the high
    ([120.00, 121.50, 125.00], 0.0),             # only rises
    ([98.40], 0.0),                              # one price
    ([100.00, 90.00, 105.00, 84.00], -0.20),     # 84 / 105 - 1, the second dip
])
def test_max_drawdown(prices, expected):
    assert max_drawdown(prices) == pytest.approx(expected)

tests.setup: planted = lambda prices: min(p / prices[0] - 1 for p in prices)
planted = lambda prices: max(1 - p / max(prices[:i + 1]) for i, p in enumerate(prices))
planted = lambda prices: min([0.0] + [p / max(prices[:i + 1]) - 1 for i, p in enumerate(prices[:-1])])
planted = lambda prices: min(p / max(prices[:i + 1]) - 1 for i, p in enumerate(prices) if i > 0)

byKey.test-1: Your test fails on the correct `max_drawdown`. Recheck each hand answer: trough over the peak before it, minus 1.

explain.text: Paths a and e catch the first-price version, and b the highest-price version. Path e also catches the skipped last day, and d the crash on one price. The signs catch the positive version. A table of cases is cheap, so give every known failure its own row.

ideas: Several asserts in one test stop at the first failure, so later cases never run.
`@pytest.mark.parametrize("x, expected", rows)` runs the test once per row, and each row reports on its own.
Give every known mistake its own row, and name the test after the behaviour it checks.

formula.name: Parametrise
formula.note: Stacked decorators combine every row with every row.

summary.trap: With one name, `parametrize("prices", [100.00, 120.00])` makes one row per float. Wrap a series in an outer list: `[[100.00, 120.00]]`.

quiz.question: How many tests does pytest run?

feedback.correct: Three series times two scales: six tests.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every row of one table meets every row of the other.

byKey.added: You added the rows. Stacked tables combine: each series runs at each scale, so 3 × 2.
byKey.outer: You counted only the series. Each series also runs at both scales.

explain.text: Stacked decorators give every combination: 3 series × 2 scales = 6 tests. Scaling every price by 100 must not change a drawdown, since it is a ratio.

quiz.prose: A test function has five `assert` lines. pytest reports that it failed on the second one.
quiz.question: How many of its `assert` lines ran?

options.why: The first one passed, so the function reached the second, which failed.
A failed assert ends the function, so lines 3 to 5 never ran.
You counted the passes you expected. Only lines 1 and 2 ran.

feedback.correct: The first passed, the second failed, and the function stopped.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A failed assert stops the function on that line.

explain.text: Asserts run top to bottom until one fails. Line 2 failed, so lines 3 to 5 tell you nothing. Rows of a parametrised test would each have run.

quiz.question: What is `prices` in the second test?

options.why: You took the rows to be single numbers. Here each item of the outer list is a whole series.
The outer list holds the rows. Each test gets one row, not all of them.

feedback.correct: The outer list holds the rows; the second row is `[80.00, 88.00]`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each item of the outer list is one row.

explain.text: With one name, each item of the list is a row. The items here are lists, so each test gets one whole series. This is the fix for the trap from the lesson.

quiz.prose: A test fails in tomorrow's run. You will see only its name in the report.
quiz.question: Which name tells you most about what broke?

options.why: A number says nothing about the behaviour. You would have to open the file to learn what failed.
'Works' covers everything, so a failure narrows nothing down.
A test of everything fails for any reason. The name cannot say which.

feedback.correct: The name states the behaviour, so the failure explains itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the name that states one behaviour.

explain.text: A name that states one behaviour turns a FAILED line into a bug report: rising prices no longer give 0. That works best with one assert per test.
